title: Eight Weeks of Reading Like an Adult
subtitle: An eight week reading plan from James Bell for the curious nonbeliever. The Bible read as literature and history, the hard objections on the table, and no tricks anywhere in it.
intro:
This is an eight week reading plan for the nonbeliever who is curious, written by a pastor who came to faith from atheism. Nothing here is a trick. There is no trap in week eight, no emotional ambush, no moment where the music swells. Each week holds one focus, one reading practice, one thing to read, one tool, and one honest question. It starts with the Gospel of Mark, read the way you'd read any ancient biography, puts the hardest objections on the table at full strength, asks what Christians actually claim, and ends with the question underneath the others. You will be asked to read carefully and to write down your real questions. You will not be asked to pray, to attend anything, or to pretend.

It isn't a cure for anything, and it isn't a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor, or the real people who can take your questions. Read it imperfectly. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up. You owe this plan nothing, and you can close it at any point with no hard feelings on this end. The only commitment it asks is the one any serious reader already makes, which is to take the text and the objections both at full strength.
careNote: If the questions bring a heaviness that reaches your sleep, appetite, or work for two weeks, or a fear of hell that brings panic, see a doctor or licensed counselor who won't push you either way. If someone at home hurts or threatens you, including over what you believe, the Domestic Violence Hotline on Find Help can help you plan for safety; in a crisis, call or text 988.

weeks.why: Before the Bible is a religious claim, it is a library: law, poetry, letters, prophecy, and four ancient lives of Jesus, written over many centuries in three languages. You can read it the way an adult reads Homer or Tacitus, owing it nothing and noticing everything. Start with Mark, the shortest of the four Gospels, before anyone explains it to you, this plan included. Notice what Jesus says and does, what the people around him get wrong, and what strikes you as strange. The strangeness is often where the real questions live.
weeks.practice: Read the Gospel of Mark this week, two or three chapters a day, so that you reach the end of chapter 16 by the week's end. Read it the way you would read any ancient text, and write down one question each sitting raises for you.

read.label: I don't believe, but I'm curious: the care page this plan walks more slowly

tool.label: Mark 1 in the Study Bible, free to read with notes on every chapter, so you need no Bible of your own

weeks.reflection: What did I expect this book to be, and where did the actual text not match the expectation?

weeks.focus: The Bible in its real world
weeks.why: This is a text from the ancient Near East and the Roman world, and a reader who brings modern American assumptions to it will misread it, whether that reader is a believer or a skeptic. A good many objections to the Bible are really objections to a culture that waves it around, and we Christians have supplied plenty of those. Sorting the two is ordinary intellectual honesty, and it makes the objections that remain sharper, not softer.
weeks.practice: Each day, reread one passage from Mark with its notes and ask what its first hearers, living under Roman rule, would have heard. When a note mentions something from their world you didn't know, look it up in the guides. Write one question a day about the gap between their world and yours.

read.label: Guides to Reading the Bible, the Study Bible's shelf on the ancient world the writers took for granted

tool.label: Mark's introduction in the Study Bible, on who wrote it, when, and the world it came from

weeks.reflection: Which of my objections are to the text itself, and which are to the modern people who use it?

weeks.focus: The violence and the slavery, on the table
weeks.why: These are serious objections, and they deserve to be treated seriously. The conquest chapters and the slavery laws are in the book, and the skeptic who refuses to look away is reading more honestly than the churchgoer who skips them. The church's own use of these texts earned some of the distrust: American preachers quoted the Bible to defend slavery, and it has been used to keep victims quiet. This week you read two chapters whose notes state the hard question plainly and give more than one answer. Keep whatever objection survives. It will at least be a precise one.
weeks.practice: Spend the first half of the week with Deuteronomy 20 and the second with Exodus 21, a few verses and their notes each day, ending with the hard question on each. Then write out the strongest objection that remains, at full strength. Nobody here will be offended by it.

read.label: Deuteronomy 20 in the Study Bible, where the hard question on the conquest gets several honest answers

tool.label: Exodus 21 in the Study Bible, where the hard question asks why the law regulates slavery instead of forbidding it

weeks.reflection: After reading the strongest case I can find, is my objection stronger, weaker, or simply more precise?

weeks.focus: Did the Gospels get Jesus right
weeks.why: The objection deserves its full strength. We don't have the original Gospels, the copies we have were made generations later, copyists made mistakes and now and then changed a word on purpose, and the four accounts differ in detail. Some of that is simply true, and you should hear it from a pastor before you find it somewhere else. What the telephone-game picture leaves out is scale and timing. The copies are many and come from many places, which is how scholars can see where a copyist slipped, and Paul, writing about twenty years after the crucifixion, passed on an older summary that names witnesses. None of that settles the question. It makes it a historical question, and historical questions deserve evidence rather than a slogan from either side.
weeks.practice: Read the guide early in the week. Then each day take one scene from Mark and ask two questions: what would have to be true for it to be invented, and what would have to be true for it to be remembered? Write a one-line verdict for each scene.

read.label: Did the Gospels Get Jesus Right? The telephone-game objection stated at full strength before it is answered

tool.label: Can I trust the Bible? The care page on what the old copies show, which concedes what is true in the skeptic's account

weeks.reflection: What standard of evidence do I apply to other ancient texts, and am I applying the same one here?

weeks.focus: Miracles, and what we decide before the evidence
weeks.why: It's easy to assume people once believed this because they knew no better, but the first audiences don't fit that story. They knew the dead stay dead, and the women's report from the tomb struck the apostles as "nonsense" (Luke 24:11). The sharper argument is modern. In his 1748 essay on miracles, David Hume argued that a wise person proportions belief to the evidence, that testimony to a miracle deserves belief only if its being false would be more miraculous than the miracle, and that no report had ever met that bar. Much of that is right; witnesses do get things wrong. But the weighing depends on a question settled before any report arrives. If there is no God, no resurrection report could be believable; if there is, it becomes a question of whether he acted. Believers and skeptics alike bring some answer to it before reading a word.
weeks.practice: Read the guide over the first few days, then the hard question at the end of Luke 24, where the skeptics' case comes first. Each day, write one sentence you actually believe about miracles and where you got it: an argument you weighed, something you inherited, or the air you grew up breathing.

read.label: Were Ancient People Gullible About Miracles? The credulity argument stated at full strength, then Hume's essay and its critics

tool.label: Luke 24 in the Study Bible, where the hard question on the resurrection states the skeptics' case first

weeks.reflection: Did I conclude that miracles are impossible, or did I inherit the conclusion, and how would I tell the difference?

weeks.why: Every tribe has tried to draft him: the left and the right, the empire and the market, and yes, the church. The man in the text keeps refusing recruitment. When the Pharisees and the Herodians tried to trap him over Caesar's tax, he answered, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's" (Mark 12:17), and before Pilate he said, "My kingdom is not of this world" (John 18:36). Whatever you eventually decide about Jesus, it should be a decision about him, not about his worst representatives. I'm a pastor, which makes me one of the representatives, and he has suffered us longer than you have.
weeks.practice: Read Mark 12 and John 18 slowly this week, a few verses a day, with the notes. Each day, write one question about Jesus himself, not about Christians or the church. Notice how much harder that is.

read.label: Mark 12 in the Study Bible, where Jesus is questioned in the temple and answers the trap about Caesar's tax

tool.label: John 18 in the Study Bible, Jesus before Pilate, with notes on whether the trial account is believable

weeks.reflection: How much of my picture of Jesus came from the text, and how much came from the people who put me off him?

weeks.focus: What Christians actually believe, against the caricature
weeks.why: You wouldn't accept a caricature of your own position, and you shouldn't be handed one of ours. You've probably met a few: a list of rules for being good, a political identity for one side or the other, a comfort for people who can't face death, a demand to believe without evidence. Christians gave you reasons to distrust every one of them, which is our fault, not yours. The church's oldest creeds say something else: one God, maker of heaven and earth; Jesus Christ, his Son, who became human, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, and rose on the third day; the forgiveness of sins; the resurrection of the body. Above that center, Christians argue openly about a great deal. This week you read the real claims and aim at those.
weeks.practice: Read the Apostles' Creed slowly, a few lines a day, with its notes. Pick the line you find least believable and write the strongest version of it you can manage, then your strongest objection to that version.

read.label: The Apostles' Creed, the full text with plain notes on what each line was answering

tool.label: Compare the Views, where Christian traditions set their disagreements side by side

weeks.reflection: If I rejected the strongest version instead of the weakest, would my rejection change in tone, in content, or not at all?

weeks.why: The loudest objections are not always the deepest ones. Underneath the violence texts and the miracles there is often something closer in: what it would cost me if this were true, and what I want to be true. Sigmund Freud built an argument on that in The Future of an Illusion (1927): belief in God answers a frightened child's wish for a protecting father, so a belief that fits our wishes this well deserves suspicion. Some faith is exactly that. But Freud granted that an illusion in his sense isn't necessarily false, though he plainly thought this one was, and the suspicion cuts both ways, since there are strong reasons to want no God at all. A pastor has wants too. In the end the question is narrower: whether a man executed under Pontius Pilate walked out of his grave, and what it would mean for you if he did.
weeks.practice: Each day, write down the question underneath your official ones, until you can say the one that is actually yours. Keep it where you will find it again. If you want company with it, find a Christian who listens well and can admit when they don't know, and ask whether you can bring hard questions without being recruited. If anyone answers with pressure or flattery, or a group asks for secrecy or money, thank them and find someone else.

read.label: 1 Corinthians 15 in the Study Bible, one of the oldest summaries of the faith, where Paul says what follows if he is wrong

tool.label: Acts 17 in the Study Bible, Paul in Athens, where some mocked and others asked to hear more

weeks.reflection: What do I want to be true, and how is that want shaping what I am able to see?
